entries.title: Cory Mills' Downfall Came From Inside the House
entries.summary: GOP leaders and the White House backed Rep. Cory Mills’ reelection bid despite a string of scandals, but one of his colleagues believed he could pose a threat to the majority.
entries.content:
As allegations of sexual misconduct, questions about his military record and campaign finance violations surrounded Florida Republican Rep. Cory Mills, House Republican leadership, the White House and the majority of the GOP conference publicly stayed behind him.

But Rep. Mike Haridopolos, a freshman member of the Florida delegation, grew concerned.

He worked behind the scenes to recruit a primary challenger in Florida’s 7th Congressional District, and despite little public support from Republican colleagues, he helped engineer Mills’ defeat.

A former president of the Florida state Senate, Haridopolos had seen this movie before. He believed Mills was more than a flawed incumbent -– he posed a threat to the majority. While Haridopolos believed Mills could fend off a primary challenge, he predicted he would struggle in the general election.

“I've been involved in Florida politics for over 25 years and within a swing seat like that, if you don't have a really solid candidate, in what could be a tough year for us, I knew it was an absolute loser,” Haridopolos told NOTUS. “And we did not want to give away a seat when we're trying to pick up seats and keep the majority.”

Mills has faced a series of controversies in the past year. NOTUS reported in 2025 about discrepancies surrounding Mills’ Bronze Star award from the Army. Army soldiers cited in the document submitting Mills for the honor said they had no recollection of Mills actually being present in the incidents listed. NOTUS also reported last year that while he was a candidate in 2021, Mills was caught with sex workers in Tbilisi, Georgia, while on a rescue mission to Afghanistan.



More recently, Mills was accused of domestic violence by one partner and separately received a restraining order from an ex-girlfriend. Both the House Ethics Committee and Department of Justice are investigating him.

Haridopolos said he believed “it was incumbent upon me” to find a candidate to take on Mills in the primary. So, he approached Ryan Elijah, a former TV news anchor.

“Ryan and I have always talked about him potentially running, and we'd had conversations and he was ready to step up and really make sure his community was well represented in Congress,” Haridopolos said. “And to his credit, he ran a really positive race and was willing to ask the tough questions.”

Elijah officially announced in April. But it was still a long-shot bid. While taking on an incumbent is always a daunting task, there were three other candidates working to knock off Mills as well that could split the vote and hurt his chances. While Haridopolos worked the ground and campaigned in Florida, back in Washington, D.C., he was also working behind the scenes.

The freshman Florida Republican took the temperature of his colleagues to determine if there was any appetite for a group to publicly come out against Mills, sources told NOTUS.

Haridopolos looped in leadership about his efforts.

“I was very candid with them from Day 1 that I felt strongly that we needed someone and they understood the situation, and they let me do what I wanted to do,” Haridopolos said.

He focused on members of his delegation and attempted to get them behind Elijah. While he only got one, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, she is arguably one of the most vocal members of the delegation.

“I have great relationships with my fellow members in the delegation, and I was just really candid with them. And I said, ‘Look, I'm just going to let you know I'm going to get involved in this race because I'm really concerned about the majority,’” Haridopolos said. “And Anna came on board and did an amazing job helping out and really elevating the conversation.”

As a freshman, campaigning against one of his delegation members could’ve caused a massive political blowback for Haridopolos if Mills would have won. But Elijah defeated Mills by 13 percentage points, and Republican leaders avoided the headache of defending an incumbent with baggage in November. He is expected to face Democratic candidate Bale Dalton in the general election, according to the Associated Press

“For the team I think this will put us in a really strong position in an R+5 seat to hold the seat without having to spend tens of millions of dollars to hold the seat,” Haridopolos said. “And we have a person that you know could hold his head up high and run a really positive campaign, and I couldn't be more thrilled.”

Haridopolos hasn’t heard from Mills since he publicly endorsed Elijah in early August and doesn’t have any plans to talk with him.

“I chose not to engage,” he said. “I wanted Ryan to stay positive and not make it about anyone but Ryan Elijah, and to his credit, again, he ran a fantastic race and his community truly lifted him up tonight.”

entries.title: Prosecutors Say Comey’s Seashell Post Became Part of His Thriller Novel’s Promo
entries.summary: A court filing compares the former FBI director’s “86 47” post to the plot of his then-forthcoming book and promotional interviews.
entries.content:
Federal prosecutors have zeroed in on James Comey’s crime thriller novel to help prove that he meant to threaten President Donald Trump’s life with his “86 47” social media post last year.

In a court filing late Monday defending their indictment, prosecutors argued that Comey knew the phrase was a call for violence against Trump in May 2025, when he posted a photo of seashells arranged with those numbers “only five days from public release” of the book.

To make the connection, prosecutors first used excerpts from the book, “FDR Drive,” which they say features a public figure who incites followers to kill his enemies through public messages.

They cited one passage describing “stochastic terrorism,” which generally refers to the use of public rhetoric to demonize a person or group: “Sean nodded. ‘It’s where a charismatic leader jacks people up but, through the wonder of the internet, avoids a direct connection to what comes next.’”

Prosecutors then continued: “On May 15, 2025, a charismatic leader named James Comey, through the wonder of the internet, posted a coded message to his followers meaning ‘kill’ or ‘get rid of’ (a euphemism for ‘kill’) President Trump.”

Prosecutors wrote that “86” was organized crime slang for kill and that “47” referred to Trump as the 47th president. “There is no serious dispute,” they wrote, “that an objective viewer of Comey’s post could read it to mean ‘Kill President Trump.’”

The filing was part of a larger batch of briefs from prosecutors responding to a sweeping attempt by Comey’s defense team to have the case thrown out. Together, they offer new insights into the government’s strategy for securing a conviction at trial, including the unorthodox approach of mining Comey’s fictional work for clues of his motive.

Comey, who has long drawn Trump’s political ire, was indicted in April on charges of threats against the president and making threats across state lines.

Defense lawyers attacked the Justice Department’s central theory of the case in hundreds of pages of filings last month, asking a judge to dismiss the indictment on the grounds that Comey’s post was not a true threat and that the Justice Department singled him out for prosecution because of his criticisms of Trump. Comey has said the message was political, not violent, and that “86” was harmless restaurant industry lingo.

In their filing Monday, prosecutors said Comey posted the image of the seashells amid a surge in violent threats and multiple assassination attempts on Trump — context, they said, that was essential for jurors to take into account at trial.

They also noted his novel centers on a federal prosecutor who takes on an extremist podcaster who uses his platform to fuel violence.Though Comey denied arranging the shells himself, prosecutors said, there was “no evidence that anyone else arranged, photographed or even saw the shells.”

Comey quickly deleted the post following outcry from Trump’s allies. Soon after, according to one filing from the government, Comey’s publishing agent sent him a text saying, “on the bright side, you’ve gone viral.” Comey replied, “Not my intention, but I’ll be OK if it sells books.” The agent texted back: “Music to an agent’s ears.”

Prosecutors detailed Comey’s media appearances to promote the novel. The filing points to a Wall Street Journal reporter asking him eight days after the post, “Is there a universe where you did this to promote your book?” to which Comey responded, “Not in a universe I live in.”

And the government also pointed to his appearance on “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.” Colbert asked about the seashell post and said: “OK, well congratulations on the attention for, for your book. There you go. That is a hell of a viral campaign.”

In a separate filing, prosecutors rejected claims by the defense that the prosecution was “vindictive” or “selective” — legal terms that refer to prosecutors charging a defendant for exercising legal rights or bringing charges that haven’t been brought against similarly situated people. Both practices are unconstitutional, but the bar for proving them in court is high.

Prosecutors said Comey had not shown that Justice Department officials involved in the case had improper motives. “Instead, he speculates that they were induced by others with

improper motives,” they wrote. Nor could he show, they said, that others in his position were not prosecuted.

Prosecutors urged the judge to deny motions by the defense to turn over grand jury records, saying they were not required to present all of Comey’s potential defenses to grand jurors who authorized the indictment.

They also said the judge should reject the defense’s request to suppress evidence and to hold a Franks hearing, in which a judge decides whether investigators lied or left out important facts to secure a search warrant. Comey’s defense team had accused the Justice Department of misleading a magistrate judge, omitting key facts and making false statements in bringing the case.

The Justice Department had previously charged Comey with lying to Congress, but a judge dismissed the case after finding the lead prosecutor, a White House appointee, had no authority to bring the charges.

entries.title: Economists Warn That Treasury’s Bond Markets Fix Is Short Term
entries.summary: Bond yields eased from 2007-level highs after the Treasury announced a new buyback operation.
entries.content:
The Trump administration responded to global anxiety around rising inflation and the war in Iran on Wednesday, making a surprise move to calm bond markets as they showed signs reminiscent of the 2007 financial crisis.

The Trump administration’s announcement — that it would be doubling its bond buybacks through early November — had almost immediate effect: Yields pulled back from record highs. But economists warn that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s course of action is only a short-term fix for a much larger problem.

“Steps like that taken this morning will prove to be a temporary salve to an open financial wound of our own making,” said Joseph Brusuelas, principal and chief economist for RSM US LLP.

The volatility of the bond market has put the administration on uneasy footing for weeks; yields on 30-year and 10-year bonds have soared, putting the U.S. economy in a dangerous position. The higher the yields, the higher the borrowing costs for homebuyers, auto loans, business investments and more, creating ripple effects across the entire economy.

On Wednesday, the Treasury Department announced it will expand its government debt buyback operation from $2 billion maximum to at least $4 billion, focusing on the 10- to 20-year and 20- to 30-year sectors. The operation, which will last from Sept. 9 through the end of the refunding quarter on Nov. 4, will buy up long-term debt and take short-term debt off the market, rebalancing the makeup of U.S. Treasury bonds on the market to reduce risks to the economy.

“This increase in buyback operation sizes reflects Treasury’s desire to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants,” the Treasury release said.

The yield on 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds this summer exceeded yields during the 2007 financial crisis, hitting 5.3% on Monday. The high yields have been attributed to global anxiety around inflation, trade wars and the war in Iran, which has left the Strait of Hormuz, a major shipping route, closed for months.

Yields above 6% pose risks to small- and medium-sized banks, because too-high yields reduce the value of bonds they’ve stockpiled. Mortgage rates, home loans and credit card payments use the 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds as a benchmark.

The Treasury’s expanded buyback operation seeks to tamp down on those high yields, potentially helping prevent bank failures and the buckling of the global economy, which is heavily reliant on U.S. government debt holdings. The yield on 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds dropped several basis points shortly after the Treasury’s announcement Wednesday morning.

While the bond market reacted quickly to the Treasury’s announcement, it’s only a temporary solution, economists warned.

Brusuelas says the buyback will not be enough to contend with the risks posed by the United States’ ballooning debt, persistent inflation and private artificial intelligence companies’ dominance.

He added that Bessent’s bond move will make Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s job of bringing inflation down to 2% harder. The inflation rate came in at 3.4% in July.

“Bessent is a political actor. His interest is purely short term and is organized around the upcoming election and not a return to price stability,” Brusuelas said. “This is what fiscal dominance looks like as the fiscal authority leans on the central bank to subordinate its goal of price stability to the government’s borrowing and political needs.”

The Treasury’s plan to buy up bonds will increase the money supply, adding to the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates to limit inflation, said Ryan Young, a senior economist at the libertarian think tank Competitive Enterprise Institute.

He characterized the unease in the bond markets as a symptom of the United States’ larger fiscal issues, including the federal debt approaching $40 trillion and looming Social Security insolvency.

“When you see story after story about multitrillion-dollar problems like that, that's going to make people a little less confident in the government's ability to repay bonds in 10 years or 30 years, so I think that's the root of the problem,” Young said.
entries.author: Jade Lozada

entries.title: Sean Duffy’s Road Trip Reality Show Premieres at Long Last
entries.summary: Critics have called for an investigation into “The Great American Road Trip,” which was first set to be released months ago.
entries.content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy released the first episode of his reality-TV-themed road trip series “The Great American Road Trip” on Wednesday, months after Duffy said it would premiere.

Duffy framed the series as his family’s way of celebrating America’s 250th birthday, but the production has sparked a number of ethical questions in recent months.

A disclaimer at the beginning of the episode says the program “is a result of an agreement between the U.S. Department of Transportation and the Great American Road Trip, Inc. Production costs — including filming, crew, food, fuel, lodging and activities — were paid for by the Great American Road Trip, Inc and accepted as a gift by the Department."

“No taxpayer dollars were spent for the participation of Secretary Duffy’s family,” the disclaimer added.

Duffy and his wife, “Fox & Friends Weekend” host Rachel Campos-Duffy, took their kids to visit Philadelphia for the inaugural episode of the series. The family kicked off their trip after visiting President Donald Trump at the White House.

“Our capital is Washington, D.C., but it all began in Philadelphia,” Campos-Duffy said.

Michael Alfonso, the 26-year-old son-in-law of the secretary, also joined the family during the episode. Alfonso won the Republican nomination last week for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District.

The family met up with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum for their first stop at Philadelphia’s Liberty Bell.

“You’re going to be stopping at a bunch of Department of the Interior sites across the country,” Burgum said to the Duffy family.

After the Liberty Bell, the family visited Independence Hall, the National Constitution Center and the Philadelphia Museum of Art — running up the same steps Sylvester Stallone traversed in the iconic “Rocky” scene. The Duffy family also spoke with an actor impersonating founding father Ben Franklin and another playing Betsy Ross, who is credited for designing the first American flag.

The disclaimer at the end of the episode states the “production was made possible by the generous support of our GART, Inc sponsors.” GART stands for Great American Road Trip.

Controversy has swirled around the series since it was announced earlier this year. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington urged the Transportation Department’s inspector general to launch a probe into Duffy’s participation in the series. Some of GART’s sponsors include some companies that the department is tasked with regulating, like aerospace company Boeing and auto manufacturer Toyota.

Five Democratic senators in June also requested for the DOT inspector general to investigate Duffy’s ties to the show.

“We are concerned with this potential mix between personal and professional activities. If the road trip was personal, then it appears a Cabinet official spent several days over multiple months taking and filming a road trip that should have been paid for by the Secretary, but instead the Secretary accepted gas, lodging, and other travel expenses from a non-profit funded by the very companies the Secretary regulates,” the senators wrote in a press release at the time.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Trump’s Governor Candidates Keep Flaming Out
entries.summary: Megan Degenfelder of Wyoming is the latest Trump-backed gubernatorial candidate who failed to secure the Republican Party’s nomination.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s chosen candidate in Wyoming’s governor’s race failed to secure the Republican nomination on Tuesday, adding to the growing list of gubernatorial candidates with Trump’s endorsement that have lost their primaries.

Megan Degenfelder, the state education superintendent endorsed by President Donald Trump, lost to state Sen. Eric Barlow on Tuesday. Others who had his backing and have lost this primary cycle are sprinkled across the U.S. They include Mike Lindell, the former MyPillow CEO of Minnesota, Rep. Randy Feenstra of Iowa, and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette of South Carolina. 

The losing streak in gubernatorial contests has raised the question of whether the president’s influence over the Republican Party is hitting its limits, an idea the White House immediately struck down.

“President Trump’s endorsement is the most powerful endorsement in the history of American politics,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told NOTUS. “Anyone claiming otherwise is a complete and utter fool.”

Several other gubernatorial candidates endorsed by the president have succeeded in becoming the nominee or advancing to the general election, including Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama, Rep. Donald Byron of Florida, and Vivek Ramaswamy of Ohio.

Still, Degenfelder’s loss to Barlow in a state that Trump won by more than 40 percentage points in 2024 demonstrates a rare instance where voters are willing to break with him.

“‘MAGA’ Megan Degenfelder has my Complete and Total Endorsement,” Trump posted on Truth Social in January.

Barlow comfortably defeated Degenfelder in the statewide race by a more than 20,000-vote margin.

The losses have come both in primaries and in runoffs, where Trump's candidates have at times failed to consolidate support after advancing from the first round.

In Georgia, Trump’s chosen candidate for governor, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, advanced to a runoff in May and then lost to business executive Rick Jackson in June.

In South Carolina, his initial pick, Evette, advanced to a runoff election in which the president ended up backing both of the Republican candidates. Evette lost in the end, though Trump was able to claim partial victory with the double endorsement.

He’s also doubled down on some of the endorsements that he has offered. In Oklahoma, which has a runoff for the Republican nomination on Aug. 25, he endorsed Mike Mazzei, a financial adviser and former state senator, two weeks before the initial primary, which took place in June.

The president has also made clear his disdain for Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, the candidate facing off against Mazzei for the state’s Republican nomination.

Trump accused Drummond of being a “FAKE Republican” as recently as Tuesday.

“Gentner Drummond has also stated publicly he had ‘no opinion’ on the BOGUS IMPEACHMENT of a young and very handsome gentleman, named, President Donald J. Trump (ME!),” Trump posted on Truth Social.

entries.title: Trump Nominates Aide Heidi Overton for FDA Commissioner
entries.summary: “Dr. Heidi has been a ROCKSTAR in my Administration,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that he is nominating Heidi Overton, a White House aide, to lead the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

“Dr. Heidi has been a ROCKSTAR in my Administration, where she has worked directly with Secretary Kennedy, Dr. Oz, and team, to deliver on the MOST TRANSFORMATIVE Health Agenda in History,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Overton, who began as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term, has served as a domestic policy adviser to the president since he returned to the White House last year. Between Trump’s terms, Overton was a chief policy officer at America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank.

If confirmed, she would succeed former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who resigned from his position May 12. He made the decision in part over his reluctance to greenlight regulatory changes at Trump’s behest that authorized the sale of flavored vapes. Shortly after NOTUS first reported Makary’s poor standing with the White House, the agency announced it was approving four new flavored vape products.

He left the agency just seven days later.

Overton is a staunch anti-abortion ally. While at the America First Policy Institute, she wrote that abortion pills were “far more dangerous to women” and advocated for restricting access, including prohibiting them from being available via mail. 

Anti-abortion leaders are confident that she could revive the long awaited FDA review of the abortion pill mifepristone that Makary had slow walked. 

“Dr. Overton is the right candidate,” John Mize, CEO of Americans United for Life, said in a statement. “She has the scientific and medical background that will enable her to perform an objective analysis of the dangers chemical abortion poses to women.” 

While mifepristone is considered safe and effective by leading medical organizations, acting FDA commissioner Kyle Diamantas has told anti-abortion advocates that he supports a safety review of abortion pills.

If confirmed, the Trump administration would have two abortion opponents overseeing abortion pill access: Overton at the FDA and Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has committed to enforcing the Comstock Act to ban abortion pills. 

Overton did not immediately respond to NOTUS’ requests for comment via text.

Trump touted Overton’s qualifications for the role in his announcement, referring to her as “a Board-Certified Physician in Public Health and General Preventive Medicine, and holds a Ph.D. in Clinical Investigations from the Johns Hopkins University.”

Overton has appeared at Trump’s side many times in recent months, including when he signed an executive order to change childhood vaccines. She stood by the president as he claimed, without evidence, that the number and rate of vaccines could play a role in autism rates — though studies have found there is no link.

To be confirmed, Overton faces a Senate with a narrow Republican majority and a confirmation hearing in the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Lousiana), the committee’s chair and a physician, has been critical of Trump and his vaccine policies, including his most recent executive order, which calls for splitting up childhood vaccines into three categories.

Republican Rep. Buddy Carter of Georgia and oncologist Jeff Vacirca were also being considered for the role, NOTUS reported earlier this week.

“Dr. Heidi Overton will perform excellently as FDA Commissioner, and I wish her success as she enacts the President’s Make America Healthy Again agenda. I am laser-focused on the work of the House and look forward to continuing to support the Trump administration, which has a mandate to put America First,” Carter said in a statement to NOTUS.

entries.title: ICE Holding San Diego Padres Coach at El Paso Detention Center
entries.summary: Immigration agents took custody of the Venezuelan national at an airport Sunday.
entries.content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement has detained a minor league baseball coach in the San Diego Padres’ organization, the club confirmed this week.

Oswaldo Pirela Dominguez, a Venezuelan national with a pending asylum application, was flying home to Arizona from the El Paso International Airport when ICE took him into custody Sunday, his family told The Athletic. He is being held at the El Paso Processing Center, according to ICE’s detainee locator system.

In a statement to multiple news outlets, the Padres organization said it was aware of Pirela Dominguez’s detainment and was working to gather more information.

Pirela Dominguez had authorization to remain in the country until February 2018, the Department of Homeland Security said in a post on X.

“In violation of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome by more than 8 YEARS,” DHS wrote. “NOBODY is above the law, and he will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”

The catching coordinator played for the Texas Rangers from 2008 to 2011 before joining the Padres staff in January 2024, according to his LinkedIn page. He worked as a landscaper and foreman in between.

Pirela Dominguez’s detention is the latest high-profile arrest at an airport as immigration agents have started arresting flyers with expired U.S. visas. ICE arrested a Cameroonian Johns Hopkins University researcher, Fatima Ameaka, at the Baltimore Washington International Airport in July. Immigration authorities released Ameaka, who has a pending asylum application and work permit, days later, ABC News reported.

entries.title: The Era of Anti-Trump Resistance Heroes Is Over
entries.summary: A string of races has shown that relying solely on an anti-Trump message may no longer be a viable winning strategy.
entries.content:
The stars of the anti-Donald Trump resistance movement that characterized much of his first presidential term failed to gain traction as they sought elected office this year amid broader upheaval in the Democratic Party over its direction and tactics.

On Tuesday, Alex Vindman, a former national security official who played a leading role in the first Trump impeachment, lost in a stunning upset to a Democratic Socialists of America member, Angie Nixon, in Florida’s Democratic Senate primary. The establishment-backed Vindman out-raised Nixon 16-to-1 and outspent her 13-to-1, yet still failed to capture the Democratic nomination to take on incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody.

This election and others like it have shown that relying solely on an anti-Trump message may no longer be a viable winning strategy.

In New York, lead Trump impeachment lawyer Rep. Dan Goldman lost his Democratic primary to a left-wing challenger, and attorney George Conway, a top Trump critic who vowed to lead Trump’s third impeachment, finished fifth in his bid for Congress. In Colorado, Rep. Diana DeGette, who played a prominent role in both Trump impeachments, lost to a progressive challenger as well.

Other prominent critics from Trump's second impeachment, which involved his efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, also lost their bids for office this year, including former U.S. Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn in Maryland; former Georgia Lt. Gov. Geoff Duncan, a Republican turned Democrat; and Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican.

Olivia Troye, a former national security adviser to Vice President Mike Pence and vocal Trump administration critic, withdrew her bid for a House seat in Virginia after the state’s Supreme Court tossed a proposed redistricting map drawn by Democrats. So did Lev Parnas, a former Trump ally turned critic, after seeking a congressional seat in Florida. Both announced they would run as Democrats.

Not every Trump resistance hero lost this year. Other impeachment managers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), who led the prosecution of Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol, easily won their primaries.

Vindman opened his campaign for Senate with a video that invoked his starring role in Trump's impeachment, one that helped him raise millions of dollars. But he failed to match Nixon’s energy and grassroots support, especially in Tallahassee, where she made a name for herself as a state representative standing up to Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis.

“Angie Nixon won because she flat hustled,” Florida Democratic strategist Steve Schale said in a blog post.

Still, it’s clear the Democratic Party is undergoing a major generational and ideological shift. Nixon is the first DSA member to win a statewide primary, and the first to be nominated for the U.S. Senate. Democratic socialist candidates have also swept to victory in a range of primaries in New York, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., capitalizing on voter frustration with the establishment and focusing heavily on economic populism.

Or, as Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) put it in a speech Wednesday at the Illinois Democratic County Chairs’ Association: “It’s not enough to just talk a good game. These are serious times that demand serious action.”

entries.title: Tarp Covering Kennedy Center Facade Must Stay, DOJ Argues in Court
entries.summary: The legal team for Rep. Joyce Beatty called it “a childish refusal” to accept Trump’s removal from the facade.
entries.content:
The tarp covering the Kennedy Center facade must remain as part of ongoing construction activities following the removal of President Donald Trump’s name from the building, Justice Department attorneys argued in a recent court filing.

Removal of the scaffolding and tarp obscuring the storied venue’s marquee will depend on the extent of required repairs, the government attorneys wrote in a Tuesday status report to the federal judge that ordered Trump’s name removed in May.

“Center management has erected one portion of this necessary scaffolding, which it used to remove President Trump’s name from the building’s facade,” the filing states. “The protective barrier around the scaffolding was and is a necessary element of the ongoing construction activities at the Center.”

The explanation comes days after the Kennedy Center’s board took a second swing at honoring the president by name, voting to carve “Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” below the official inscription honoring Kennedy. The new resolution would also name the grounds of the center the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

The board also voted on Aug. 13 to shut down the center for two years to carry out an extensive $250 million renovation project.

The legal team representing ex officio member Rep. Joyce Beatty shot back at the DOJ’s assertions in the same report, calling it a “pretextual justification.”

“Congress established the Center as a tribute to President Kennedy,” Beatty’s attorneys wrote. “His name should once again be visible on the façade and Defendants’ childish refusal to accept this Court’s ruling to that effect should end now.”

They’re asking the court to demand further explanation on why the tarp shouldn’t be removed within 30 days.

entries.title: The Incredible Baseball Life of Tommy John
entries.summary: The pitcher, who died last week, is remembered for a groundbreaking procedure. But he was much more than that.
entries.content:
Tommy John won 288 games the old-time way with his brain as much as his two left elbows.

When John passed away on Saturday at 83, the sports world remembered Tommy John surgery. That’s the elbow ligament replacement operation performed on him in ’74 by Dodgers team physician Frank Jobe. Before the knife, John won 124 games. After, he won 164 more, including all three of his 20-win seasons and all three of his trips to the World Series, where he had a 2.67 ERA.

Now, about 36% to 39% of MLB pitchers have had “TJ surgery.” You miss a season, come back with a new elbow, which, on average, lasts eight years. It’s a second life. You may throw a little worse than before, or better.

I’m lucky. I remember Tommy John himself, one of my favorite players to chat with during the last decade-plus of his 26 seasons. John was funny, self-deprecating and loved by everyone. As his career victory total climbed but seemed destined to stop short of 300 wins and an almost inevitable invitation trip to Cooperstown, John never obsessed over whether he’d make it. He’d been mediocre for his first eight years and played for six teams. He’d been released and once even retired to coach high school ball. Jobe told him the odds for success on his elbow surgery were “1,000-to-1.” Once, he asked to pitch for his friend’s semi-pro team.

So, when he hung on late in his career it was because … you never know. At 43, he discovered lifting weights — every day, even on mornings when he would pitch that night. “I discovered all those ‘lat’ muscles in the back below the shoulder,” he said. “I wasn’t even using them.”

“He never threw hard, but now he’s [back] throwing just as not-hard as he ever did,” said Yankees bullpen coach Jeff Torborg.

At 44, John went 13-6 and led the pennant-contending Yankees in innings pitched. That year I asked him if this was a 300-win quest.

“The only thing that burns inside me,” he said, “is Szechuan food.”

Modesty was core to his upbringing in Terre Haute, Indiana. A multisport star in high school, John was recruited to go to national powerhouse Kentucky to play basketball. He was also valedictorian of his class. But he didn’t give a graduation speech because of a stammer.

Tommy John AP - 790903086 (3000x2101, AR: 1.43)
Perhaps that led to some of his egoless affect as an adult. But that problem also fed into his passion for self-improvement. He eventually became one of the game’s chatterbox tale-tellers.

Tommy John even liked to tell the truth. Asked about his repertoire, he said, “I have a fastball, curveball, slider and changeup — as well as eight other illegal pitches.”

“Can I quote you?” I asked him. Tommy just grinned his friendly, innocent, church deacon smile. Pitchers love hitters thinking they cheat.

Give John a ball with a scuff or scrape and he could make its gyroscope go on the fritz just before it got to the plate. Give him a perfect ball and … well … who knows what might befall it.

When pitcher Rick Rhoden was frisked by umps in search of sandpaper, John suggested that he leave notes in his glove for the umps that said, “Right church. Wrong pew.” Or: “Warmer.”

John’s fastball never touched 90. But his pitching IQ may’ve been twice that. He drove hitters crazy, especially as, with age, he seemed to be tossing batting practice.

The excellent Baltimore Oriole teams could seldom anticipate what, or where, his next pitch would be. He seemed to follow no pattern or logic. Most frustrating, he would get into jams, then escape by getting hitters to chase low pitches and hit grounders, often into double plays.

How did he do it?

“You can’t write this until after I retire,” John said. Then he explained that all pitchers and hitters focus on “the count.” The strategy for the next pitch is usually based on that count. When pitchers get behind, like 2-0, 3-1 or 3-2, they want to avoid throwing another “ball” and getting further behind.

Hitters get aggressive when they are “ahead in the count,” especially with men on base. They think they’ll get a more hittable pitch.

“I subtract one ball from the count on the scoreboard,” said John. “If it says ‘3-1’ on the scoreboard, then it says ‘2-1’ to me.

“How is the hitter going to ‘think along with me’ if he doesn’t even know what the count is?”

John did not think “ball three” existed. For him, it was never more than two. So, he never “gave in” to the hitter. For him, every aim was at an edge or a few inches off it. He’d start with “strike one,” then you might never see another.


Because of his control, combined with the natural over-anxiousness of most hitters, plus his “subtract one ball” idea, John pitched hitters tougher, more to the edges or even off the edge, the more men got on base. The worse the jam, the more he counted on you to get yourself out.

“There’s always a base open somewhere,” said John, meaning that if he issued a walk, he’d just apply his methods to the next hitter.

“What if the bases are loaded and it’s a 3-2 pitch?” I asked. “Then there’s no ‘open base.’”

“Home plate is always open,” John said.

You might get a run with “ball four,” but not two, three or four runs with one swing.

Sure, some could “wait him out.” Not many.

Tommy John AP - 7907170216 (3000x2110, AR: 1.42)
Ironically, John’s best-known pitch may be the one that was hit the furthest. In 1966, Tommy gave up Frank Howard’s legendary upper-deck home run to center field in RFK Stadium, one of the longest home runs ever. The seat it hit was painted white. For years, players visiting D.C. would ask me, “Where was home plate then?” “Right where it is now,” I’d say. Few seemed to believe.

“It was a line drive. I almost jumped for it,” John told me. Then John turned and claimed that he could “see it rising.” By the time he got to the dugout, he said he looked like a ghost. “If it had hit me, it would have killed me.”

In the previous inning, John had hit a home run himself. He never mentioned that.

Among all pitchers, John may be the most overlooked for his accomplishments because he is remembered for his incredible dogged longevity and for his scar. But facts, especially in appreciations like this, are fine friends. Since 1900, John ranks seventh in starts, 14th in innings pitched and 18th in wins. Read that again.

Twice, he was second for the Cy Young Award. Across 88.1 postseason innings, he was 6-3 with a 2.65 ERA. In 1968, he was an All-Star with a 1.98 ERA, using all original parts. His 3.34 career ERA tops Roy Halladay and Phil Niekro and is just behind Justin Verlander and John Smoltz. John: 26 seasons. The record: 27.

His Hall of Fame voting topped at 31%, far below the 75% needed. Why?

In part, it was because his self-deprecating personality and unflashy performance deflected attention. He only won 15 games five times — back when wins “mattered.” No-hitters: zero. Rings: none. Season leading the league in ERA, wins or strikeouts: none.

One year, he induced eight ground balls for every time he got a strikeout. In 700 starts, he only allowed 302 homers. You were safe in the bleachers, but he was death on worms in the infield dirt. Come see Tommy, and get bored.

In 1980, John won 22 games, his most ever, with 16 complete games, six shutouts and 265 innings. Take 20 guesses at his strikeout total: It was 78.

So, I’m happy they named the darn surgery after Tommy John, instead of Dr. Jobe, even though he may have been a medical genius.

Plenty of people are in Cooperstown who will be almost entirely forgotten. But as long as pitchers grab their elbow and leave the mound disconsolate, fans’ll say, “He’ll probably make it back. Tommy John showed them all the way.”

Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Aug. 19, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Many Federal Reserve officials think the central bank could hike interest rates if inflationary pressures do not recede, according to newly released minutes from their July meeting.

Alex Vindman, who played a leading role in the first impeachment case, lost in a major upset to Angie Nixon in Florida’s Democratic Senate primary — the latest example this cycle that shows centering a campaign on protesting the president could be a losing strategy.

  • Senate HELP Chair Bill Cassidy says he has “strong concerns” about her nomination. “Dr. Overton’s active role in last week’s nonsensical vaccine executive order” in itself “is almost disqualifying,” the Louisiana Republican wrote on X.
Sean Duffy dropped the first episode of his reality TV-themed series today — months after the transportation secretary said it would premiere.

The tarp covering the Kennedy Center’s facade must stay up, the DOJ argued in a recent court filing, calling the “protective barrier” a “necessary element of the ongoing construction activities.”

Federal prosecutors argue in a new court filing that James Comey knew the “86 47” social media post was a call for violence against Trump, using excerpts from his novel, “FDR Drive.”

ICE detained a minor league baseball coach with the San Diego Padres this week.

entries.title: Judge Blocks Trump’s Abstinence-Only Overhaul of Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program
entries.summary: The court, however, declined to reinstate any of the funding that had already been cut.
entries.content:
A federal judge halted the Trump administration’s recent abstinence-only overhaul of the federally funded Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program on Wednesday, throwing a wrench into the White House’s plan to accomplish a long-held goal of American conservatives.

Chistopher Cooper, a federal judge in Washington, ruled against the administration’s sweeping grant cuts to sex education programs in order to favor abstinence-only education.

“Millions of American teenagers have sex,” Cooper wrote, matter-of-fact, in the opening line of his decision.

“Alarmed by the country’s rising teenage birth rate, Congress funded grants through the Teen Pregnancy Prevention (‘TPP’) Program to support local initiatives proven to reduce teen pregnancy, as well as promising approaches that might also prove effective after further observation and study,” Cooper wrote, also saying that Congress intended for these programs to “employ a range of strategies, from encouragement of abstinence and delayed sexual activity to education about contraceptives.”

Cooper also wrote that Health and Human Services had imposed conditions on grant recipients that were unreasonable, unexplained or that Congress did not intend.

HHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The program was established by Congress in 2010 to fund evidence-based sexual health curricula. The first Trump administration attempted to shorten grant periods and redirect funding toward abstinence-only-until-marriage approaches, but that triggered legal pushback from public health advocates.

In June, HHS abruptly canceled 53 out of 67 existing TPP grants — totaling roughly $68 million — citing “misalignment with agency priority” and defunding university, health department and Planned Parenthood programs across many states.

In July, the administration introduced a replacement framework shifting resources toward “reproductive goals counseling,” anatomy, fertility tracking, and abstinence rather than contraceptives.

Also in July, a coalition of organizations and local governments filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging HHS violated federal law by ignoring Congress' statutory mandate that the program’s funds be guided by medical and scientific evidence, not political ideology.

The court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs on the curriculum of these sex education programs and grant requirements, but did not reinstate any of the previously cut funding “because of lingering uncertainty over the Court’s power to order such relief.”

entries.title: Darline Graham’s Campaign Must Give Back Megadonor Money
entries.summary: Federal regulators flagged donations to the Republican senator from prominent executives, attorneys and former ambassadors.
entries.content:
In the days after Darline Graham was sworn into her late brother’s Senate seat, a parade of chief executives, lobbyists and other prominent Republican donors contributed thousands of dollars each to her campaign for a full term in the Senate.

Some opened their pocketbooks a little too wide.

Graham’s nascent Senate campaign received more than $24,000 worth of contributions over the legal limit in the course of a single week, according to a letter the Federal Election Commission sent the campaign on Monday.

The list of flagged donors is an eminent who’s who of powerful business and political figures. There’s Charles R. Schwab, the chair and founder of brokerage giant Charles Schwab; David H. Wilkins, the former U.S. ambassador to Canada and former speaker of the South Carolina House; and Ziad S. Ojakli, the head of public policy at TikTok.

The FEC also flagged donations from the leaders of Blackstone, AmTrust, Micco Corporation, Westrock Capital Partners, The Daschle Group, Newtek Business Services and NRx Defense Systems. Sen. Lisa Murkowski's Denali Leadership PAC also donated $5,000 over the legal limit, according to the FEC.

Individual donors may give a federal-level political candidate up to $3,500 per election, including primaries, runoffs and general election campaigns, according to FEC rules.

Graham’s campaign materialized quickly after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, died suddenly on July 11. She was sworn in to his seat three days later and declared her candidacy on July 23 for a full six-year term. The donations flagged by regulators all occurred between July 29 and Aug. 5.

The campaign, which did not immediately return a request for comment, now must refund or redesignate the excess funds — roughly 10% of her cash on hand, which stood at more than $251,000 as of Aug. 5.

The Senate race is headed for an Aug. 25 runoff between Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman, whose month-old Senate campaign hasn’t received any similar attention from the FEC so far.

The pair of Republican candidates debated on Tuesday, with Graham stumbling over a question about Taiwan’s importance to U.S. interests.

“National security is not my thing,” Graham said. “I’m not a polished politician up here.”

Other high-profile political candidates have also accepted excessive donations that federal law required them to return.

Among them: James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, who NOTUS reported must give back more than $1 million.

entries.title: Rep. Jimmy Gomez Accuser Says Their Interactions Were Nonconsensual
entries.summary: The representative faces a House Ethics investigation over sexual misconduct allegations.
entries.content:
An anonymous woman told the House Ethics Committee that her interactions with Rep. Jimmy Gomez were not “consensual in nature,” her attorneys said in a statement.

On Monday, the committee launched an investigation into the California Democrat based on allegations of sexual harassment and assault. He’s one of several House lawmakers to face an ethics probe related to sexual misconduct accusations this session.

“Congress must act to rein in its members who seem to believe that preying on young women working on Capitol Hill is one of the perks of their job,” attorneys Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt wrote in a joint statement on Wednesday, calling Gomez’s actions the “latest example of brazen sexual misconduct” on the Hill.

A Gomez spokesperson said they had no comment on the attorneys’ statement and referred NOTUS to a previous statement by Gomez: “Out of respect for my family and the ongoing process, I will have no further comment.”

The committee’s investigation into Gomez includes allegations of sexual misconduct with a House staffer. Under the House Ethics code of conduct, members of Congress are not explicitly forbidden from pursuing relationships with staffers outside of their office or committee assignments — a rule that some members want to see changed. Members cannot have relationships with staffers within their own office or committees.

“Although my actions were consensual in nature and haven't violated the law or House Ethics rules, that doesn't diminish the impact that these mistakes have made on those I care about the most,” Gomez said in a statement Monday after the committee announced its investigation.

The anonymous woman’s attorneys refuted Gomez’s claims that his conduct was “consensual in nature” in their statement Wednesday.

It’s unclear whether the woman in question was a member of Gomez’s own staff or worked in another congressional office. The attorneys told NOTUS they could not reveal additional information about her role in Congress.

In April, the New York Post reported that Gomez had been seen kissing an aide from another representative’s office at a party hosted by former Rep. Eric Swalwell in 2023. Gomez, who is married, founded the Congressional Dads Caucus that same year.

While investigating the 2023 allegation, the committee uncovered other accusations, sources told CNN in June.

Gomez was close to Swalwell and Sen. Ruben Gallego while all three served in the House. In the past year, Swalwell suspended his gubernatorial campaign, which Gomez formerly chaired, and stepped down from Congress following accusations of sexual misconduct. Gallego and Gomez have since been questioned about their relationship with Swalwell while also facing scrutiny over their conduct with other staffers.

Gomez is one of several House lawmakers from both sides of the aisle who face ethics investigations and pressure to resign from office or give up their reelection campaigns.

Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) stepped down this year after admitting to a relationship with a former staffer. Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-North Carolina) ended his reelection campaign amid accusations of inappropriate behavior toward female staffers. Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) demanded an investigation into himself over allegations of domestic and child abuse. And Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida), who is currently under investigation, lost his primary on Tuesday to a former television news anchor.
